name: Appealmaxxing

lead: Appealmaxxing is a term from looksmaxxing forums for working on overall sexual or social appeal as distinct from measurable facial structure. Where 'PSL' style rating focuses on bones and proportions, appeal is treated as the broader impression a person makes, which grooming, style and body can change.

Community guides present it as the more changeable side of attractiveness: a good haircut, tidy eyebrows and facial hair, flattering glasses, skin care and physique are the usual levers. No formal research is tied to the term itself, so the guidance is largely members' own experience.

paras: Guides split the topic into face and body. On the face, members list hair (often called 'makeup for men'), grooming of eyebrows, stubble or beard, and glasses that suit the wearer. Body-focused advice covers training and presentation. People typically experiment with styles and keep what draws a better response.

The practice is low risk in itself, being mostly haircuts, grooming and clothing. Members themselves caution that a poor haircut can lower appeal as readily as a good one can raise it, and that guides differ in quality.

lead: Appealmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for raising how attractive and likeable a person comes across overall, mainly through the parts of appearance that can be changed without altering bone structure: hair, grooming, eyebrows, facial hair, glasses, skin, physique and style.[1] Forum authors present it as a separate target from conventional face ratings, which they say focus on bones and proportions.[1][2]

The idea sits inside the "softmaxxing" side of looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia describes as non-invasive practices such as skincare, grooming, clothing choices and fitness, in contrast to "hardmaxxing" interventions such as drugs or surgery.[2] In a widely referenced looksmax.org guide, the author splits appeal into facial and body components, calls facial appeal the hardest to improve, and says some factors can be adjusted depending on a person's facial phenotype and archetype. The first levers listed are hair, grooming and glasses.[1]

The term is community vocabulary rather than a research construct, and no published studies test "appealmaxxing" as such. Researchers have, however, studied some of the individual levers it names, including preferences for beards and stubble.[3]
infobox: Grooming, hair, glasses, facial hair, body, style

paras: Appealmaxxing refers to raising how attractive a person comes across overall instead of improving a single feature. Guide authors frame it as separate from bone-structure-based ratings and as something a person with an unremarkable facial structure can still work on.[1]

Looksmaxxing itself is described by Wikipedia as an online self-improvement practice aimed at maximising men's physical attractiveness, with the term originating on forums in the 2010s and spreading to TikTok and other platforms in the 2020s. The PSL scale, which ranks looks numerically, came out of the same forums.[2] Appealmaxxing is one of the vocabulary items that grew up alongside it, used by members who want advice on presentation rather than on bones or surgery.

The looksmax.org guide divides the topic into face and body. For the face it lists three starting points: hair, proper grooming (eyebrow shape and slits, stubble, a full beard or a goatee) and glasses.[1] The body half of the guide is mentioned by the author but the visible text of the thread concentrates on the face.[1]

The author describes hair as "makeup for men" that can change appeal substantially, while saying it cannot move someone up two or three tiers and that roughly one tier is the ceiling. They also warn that a poor haircut can damage appeal, so the lever works in both directions.[1] On glasses, the author tells readers not to accept the view that frames on the face are unattractive, saying some men suit them and that frames can help hide a weak eye area.[1]

Facial hair is one lever where published psychology exists. A 2023 online survey of 509 Polish men asked them to rate clean-shaven, light stubble, heavy stubble and full-beard versions of a morphed face. Men with heavy stubble or full beards wanted more facial hair on themselves than on other men, and facial hair was rated as more appropriate in informal than in formal settings, especially with unfamiliar men.[3]

The authors interpret beards as a form of impression management and note limits: four beard categories, one face model, a single country and self-reported attitudes rather than behaviour. The study did not test whether beards change how attractive a man is judged to be.[3] Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness summarises other work on body hair, shaving and body shape, but none of it is specific to the appealmaxxing framework.[4]

Within the forum guide the main claims are that hair gives a solid one-tier lift, that grooming of eyebrows and beards can "make or break" a face, and that glasses suit some men and can mask a weaker eye area.[1] Replies to the guide were mixed: one member called it a good thread but "mostly water", while the author said they planned to share further personal methods.[1]

Wikipedia notes that men's magazines long promoted skincare, hairstyle and grooming advice that overlaps with softmaxxing, and that the wider looksmaxxing scene has drawn criticism from commentators who tie it to incel culture and body-image concerns.[2] Appealmaxxing is among the milder parts of that scene, since its levers are haircuts, grooming and clothing. Members themselves describe it as the changeable side of attractiveness, in contrast to jaw or eye-area structure.[1]
No studies found. Related research on preferences for men's facial hair exists but does not test appealmaxxing as a package.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, appealmaxxing is discussed in guide threads that list grooming and styling steps for improving how attractive a person comes across, usually with a stated aim of changing impressions without changing bone structure.[1]
